title: Number patterns: what comes next?

summary.text: A staircase of chana has 1, then 2, then 3, then 4. How many will the seventh step have? You can know before you build it. You will build staircases, hop along a number track, put down kolam dots and say a chant that grows. You will learn to find the rule of a number pattern, carry it on, run it backwards and find a missing number. You will also see how far one small step can take you.
summary.art: A girl kneeling on a kitchen floor laying chana in a staircase of rows, 1, 2, 3 and 4, with a small heap ready for the next row.

intro.hook: How many dots will step 5 have?
intro.text: Step 5 will have 5 dots. Each step has one more dot than the step before. That is the rule of this pattern. When you know the rule, you can say what comes next without seeing it. In this unit you will find the rules of number patterns with chana, hops and claps.
intro.art: Four rows of chana on a floor, 1, 2, 3 and 4 long, with a child's hand holding more chana above an empty fifth row.

outcomes: I can carry on a number pattern that goes up by one or by two each time.
I can carry on a number pattern that goes down by one or by two each time.
I can say the rule of a pattern: what changes each time.
I can find a missing number or a wrong number in a pattern.
I can build a number pattern as a staircase and show it on a number track.
I can tell whether a pattern grows, shrinks or repeats.

terms.meaning: A row of numbers that follows a rule.
terms.example: 2, 4, 6, 8 is a number pattern. Each number is two more than the one before.
terms.art: The numbers 2, 4, 6, 8 in a row with a curved arrow marked '2 more' between each pair.

terms.meaning: What you do each time to get the next number.
terms.example: In 1, 2, 3, 4 the rule is one more each time.
terms.art: A staircase of dots with a small '+1' written on each step up.

terms.meaning: How much the pattern changes each time. It is the size of the jump.
terms.example: In 3, 5, 7 the step is two. You jump over one number each time.
terms.art: A number track with a counter jumping from 3 to 5 to 7.

terms.meaning: A pattern where the numbers get bigger each time.
terms.art: Four rows of chana, each one longer than the row above.

terms.meaning: A pattern where the numbers get smaller each time.
terms.example: 10, 8, 6, 4 shrinks by two each time. There are two fewer each time.
terms.art: Four rows of chana, each one shorter than the row above.

terms.meaning: One more is the next number when you count on. One fewer is the number just before.
terms.example: One more than 6 is 7. One fewer than 6 is 5.
terms.art: A row of six chana with one extra being added, and another row of six with one being taken away.

terms.meaning: Rows of things laid one under the other, where each row is longer or shorter by the same amount.
terms.example: Rows of 1, 2, 3 and 4 chana make a staircase that grows by one.
terms.art: Chana laid in rows of 1, 2, 3 and 4, lined up on the left like stairs.

terms.meaning: A strip of boxes with the numbers written in order, one in each box.
terms.example: You put a button on 0 and hop it two boxes at a time: 2, 4, 6.
terms.art: A paper strip of boxes numbered 0 to 20 with a button on 6.

terms.meaning: A number left out of a pattern. The rule tells you what it is.
terms.art: The row 4, 5, an empty box, 7, with a magnifying glass over the empty box.

explanations.concept: A number pattern has a rule
explanations.context: This card says what a number pattern is. You built one in the Staircase Test.
explanations.definition: A number pattern is a row of numbers that follows a rule. The rule says what to do each time to get the next number.
explanations.description: Look at the rows of dots: 1, 2, 3, 4. Each row has one more dot than the row above. 'One more each time' is the rule. A rule needs a start too. This pattern starts at 1. If you know the start and the rule, you can make the whole pattern yourself. Try it: start at 5, one more each time. You get 5, 6, 7, 8.
examples: Start at 1, one more each time: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
Start at 2, two more each time: 2, 4, 6, 8.
Start at 10, one fewer each time: 10, 9, 8, 7.
explanations.art: A staircase of dots, 1, 2, 3 and 4, with the words 'start at 1' at the top and '+1' beside each new row.

explanations.context: This card is about the simplest growing pattern. It is the one you make every time you count.
explanations.definition: In a 'one more' pattern, each number is the next counting number.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. The pattern is 6, 7, 8. What comes next? One more than 8 is 9, so 9 comes next. A 'one more' pattern can start anywhere. Counting itself is this pattern: 1, 2, 3, 4, and on for ever. Now you try: 12, 13, 14. What comes next?
examples: The stairs in a house: each stair is one more than the last.
Your age: one more each birthday.
13, 14, 15, 16: one more each time, starting at 13.
explanations.art: A row of chana six long, then seven, then eight, each row with its last chana coloured differently to show the one that was added.

explanations.context: This card is about patterns that go up in jumps of two. You hopped them on the number track.
explanations.definition: In a 'two more' pattern, each number is two more than the one before. You jump over one number each time.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. Put a button on 2 on the number track and hop two boxes. You land on 4, then 6, then 8. The pattern is 2, 4, 6, 8, and you jumped over 3, 5 and 7. Now start on 1 with the same rule. You get 1, 3, 5, 7. The rule is the same, but the start is different, so the numbers are different.
examples: Shoes by the door: 2, 4, 6, 8, one pair at a time.
The right-hand pages of most books: 1, 3, 5, 7.
Climbing stairs two at a time: you land on 2, 4, 6.
explanations.art: A number track from 0 to 10 with curved hops from 2 to 4 to 6 to 8, and the jumped-over boxes 3, 5 and 7 shaded lightly.

explanations.concept: Shrinking patterns: one fewer, two fewer
explanations.context: This card is about patterns that get smaller each time. You built one in the Staircase Test, starting from 9.
explanations.definition: In a shrinking pattern, each number is smaller than the one before, by the same amount each time.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. Five idlis are on a plate, and you eat one at a time. The pattern is 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0. The rule is one fewer each time. A pattern can also go down in twos: 10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 0. With chana, a shrinking pattern stops when nothing is left. A shrinking pattern is a growing pattern read from the other end. Read 5, 4, 3 backwards and you get 3, 4, 5.
examples: A countdown: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, zero.
A lift going down: 4, 3, 2, 1.
Twelve murukkus, two eaten each day: 12, 10, 8, 6.
explanations.art: Rows of idlis on plates, five, then four, then three, then two, then one, then an empty plate.

explanations.context: This card shows how to find the rule of a number pattern that someone else made.
explanations.definition: To find the rule, look at two numbers side by side. Ask: did it go up or down, and by how much? Then check another pair, because one pair alone can trick you.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. The pattern is 3, 5, 7, 9. Step 1: is it going up or down? It is going up. Step 2: how far is it from 3 to 5? Hop it on the number track: two hops. Step 3: check the other pairs. From 5 to 7 is two, and from 7 to 9 is two, so the rule is two more each time.
examples: 8, 9, 10: up by one each time. The rule is one more.
14, 12, 10: down by two each time. The rule is two fewer.
1, 2, 4: up by one, then up by two. The step is not the same, so the rule is not 'one more'.
explanations.art: A number track with a finger hopping from 3 to 5, and small arcs marked '2' between 3 and 5, 5 and 7, and 7 and 9.

explanations.concept: Finding a missing number or a wrong number
explanations.context: This card shows how to use the rule to find a number that is missing from a pattern, or one that is wrong.
explanations.definition: A missing number is found by using the rule from the number before it. A wrong number is found the same way: say the pattern by the rule, and stop where the written number does not match.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. The pattern is 4, 6, __, 10. Step 1: find the rule from two numbers side by side. From 4 to 6 is two more. Step 2: use the rule. Two more than 6 is 8. Step 3: check with the next number. Two more than 8 is 10, so 8 fits.
examples: 7, 8, __, 10: the missing number is 9.
9, 7, __, 3: the rule is two fewer, so the missing number is 5.
2, 4, 5, 8: the 5 is wrong. Two more than 4 is 6.
explanations.art: A staircase of chana with one row hidden under a folded cloth, and a child pointing at the rows above and below it.

explanations.context: This card sorts patterns into three kinds. It helps you tell a number pattern that grows from a pattern that only repeats.
explanations.definition: A repeating pattern has a part that comes again and again. A growing pattern gets bigger each time. A shrinking pattern gets smaller each time.
explanations.description: Clap, stamp, clap, stamp is a repeating pattern. The part 'clap, stamp' comes again and again, and it never gets bigger. Now clap once, then twice, then three times. That is a growing pattern, because each turn is one clap more. To tell them apart, ask one question. Does the same part come again, or does it change by a step each time? In the picture, the row of beads repeats.
explanations.art: Top: beads in a row, red, blue, red, blue. Below: rows of one, two and three beads.

explanations.concept: Number patterns in the sky and in your day
explanations.context: This card looks for growing and shrinking patterns outside the maths book: on your birthday, in a lift and on the Moon.
explanations.definition: Many things around us go up or down in steps. Some keep exactly the same step. Some only roughly.
explanations.description: Your age is a 'one more' pattern: you were 5, you are 6, you will be 7. The days left until a festival are a 'one fewer' pattern: 3 days, 2 days, 1 day, today. These steps are exact, because people count them. Now look at the Moon. After the new moon, the bright part grows a little each night for about two weeks. Then it shrinks a little each night for about two weeks. But it does not change by exactly the same amount each night. The tidy rule, the same step every time, belongs to counting.
examples: A lift going up shows 1, 2, 3, 4.
A countdown before a rocket leaves Sriharikota: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0.
The Moon: thin, then a little wider each night until full, then a little thinner each night.
explanations.art: A row of seven Moons from a thin crescent to a full circle, above a child marking days off on a wall calendar.

explanations.concept: A teak tree and a coconut palm keep a pattern too
explanations.context: This card is about two living beings who grow by one small step at a time, and what scientists have found.
explanations.description: Cut across the trunk of a teak tree and you see rings, one inside the other. A teak tree grows fast in the rains and very slowly in the dry months. That makes one ring of wood each year. So a teak who is 10 years old has about 10 rings, and one who is 30 has about 30. Scientists in India count teak rings to learn about the rains of long ago. A coconut palm opens about one new leaf each month, 12 to 14 in a year. Each old leaf leaves a ring-shaped scar on the trunk when it falls. People do not agree on what to call this.
examples: One more year, one more ring: 1, 2, 3, 4.
In a very odd year a teak can make an extra ring, so scientists check many trees against each other.
A coconut palm with poor soil or little water opens fewer leaves in a year.

perspectives.who: The view that the tree is keeping the pattern
perspectives.explanation: A tree senses the rains and the dry months, and grows or rests in answer. Year after year they add one ring. The tree is doing something step by step, in their own body. It is a number pattern made without number words.

A ring is a mark left by the seasons. The tree is not counting anything. People count the rings afterwards. And the pattern is rough: a ring can be wide or thin, and now and then there is one too many or one too few.

explanations.art: A cut teak log showing clear rings from the centre outward, beside a tall coconut palm whose trunk shows ring-shaped leaf scars.

chart.title: Rings in a young teak, year by year

explanations.concept: Stretch: when the step itself grows
explanations.context: This card goes further than Class 1. It is for a child who finds 'one more' and 'two more' easy.
explanations.definition: In some patterns the step is not the same each time. The step has a pattern of its own.
explanations.description: Build a staircase of chana with rows of 1, 2, 3 and 4. After each row, count all the chana so far. The totals go 1, 3, 6, 10. Look at the steps between them: two more, then three more, then four more. The step grows by one each time. So the next total is five more than 10, which is 15. About 1,500 years ago the Indian mathematician Aryabhata wrote down a quick rule for adding numbers that go up in equal steps.
examples: Ten bowling pins stand in rows of 1, 2, 3 and 4.
explanations.art: Four staircases of chana side by side, with 1, 3, 6 and 10 chana in all, and the totals written under them.

agreed.text: If you know where a pattern starts and what its rule is, you can work out every number in it.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it. Tell two people 'start at 3, two more each time'. Both will write 3, 5, 7, 9, without seeing each other's paper.

agreed.text: When you count 1, 2, 3, 4, you are making a number pattern. Its rule is one more each time.
agreed.evidence: Lay chana in rows as you count. Each row is one longer than the row before. That is the staircase.

agreed.text: If you start at 2 and go up by two each time, you never land on 1, 3, 5 or 7.
agreed.evidence: Hop it on a number track with a button. The button jumps over every second box, and it is always the same boxes.

agreed.text: A teak tree usually adds one ring of wood each year.
agreed.evidence: A forester named Dietrich Brandis reported yearly rings in teak in 1879. Scientists in India still use teak rings to work out which years were dry and which were wet.

challenging.claim: To find the tenth number in a pattern, you must write out all nine numbers before it.
challenging.context: This card is about a claim that sounds sensible. It asks whether there is a quicker way than writing everything out.
challenging.for: Writing them all out always works, and it is the safest way when a pattern is new to you.
challenging.against: Often the rule gives a short cut. In 1, 2, 3, 4 the tenth number is simply 10. In 2, 4, 6, 8 the tenth number is ten twos, which is 20. Mathematicians look for short cuts like these.

challenging.claim: If a pattern begins 2, 4, the next number must be 6.
challenging.context: This card asks whether two numbers are enough to be sure of a rule.
challenging.for: Two more each time is the simplest rule that fits, and it is what most people mean.
challenging.against: Another rule fits too. Add the number to itself each time: 2 and 2 is 4, and 4 and 4 is 8. With that rule, 8 comes next. Two numbers fit more than one rule. That is why you check more pairs.

challenging.who: An old idea, held by many people who love maths
challenging.context: This card asks whether the neat rule 'the same step every time' is really out there in trees and in the sky.
challenging.for: A teak tree adds a ring a year. The Moon grows and shrinks on time, month after month. Rules like these let people make calendars.
challenging.against: Look closely and the steps are never exactly the same. Rings are wide in wet years and thin in dry years. The Moon's bright part does not grow by the same amount each night. The exact rule is in our counting. Nature comes close to it.

big_questions.q: You know step 100 of the 'one more' staircase has 100 chana. Nobody has built it. How can you know?
big_questions.hint: What does the rule tell you about every step?

big_questions.q: Is there a last number in the pattern 2, 4, 6, 8?
big_questions.hint: Take the biggest one you can say. Can you add two?

big_questions.q: Can a pattern go down for ever, the way it can go up for ever?
big_questions.hint: With chana it stops at none. Ask a grown-up about the numbers on a very cold thermometer.

big_questions.q: You are taller than you were last year. On which day did it happen?
big_questions.hint: Was there one big day? Or many tiny ones?

big_questions.q: A teak tree adds one ring each year. Is the tree doing maths?
big_questions.hint: The tree has no number words. Does a pattern need words?

big_questions.q: Who made the rule 'one more each time': people, or the world?
big_questions.hint: Think of the chana staircase. Then think of the Moon.

story.title: The Lamp That Went Out
story.note: Nila, Kannan and their grandmother are made up. Karthigai Deepam is a real festival of lamps, kept in Tamil Nadu in the Tamil month of Karthigai, when families light rows of small clay lamps outside their homes.
text: It was the evening of Karthigai Deepam, and the whole street smelled of oil and wicks.
Nila was seven. Her cousin Kannan was five, and he had come all the way from Coimbatore just for the lamps.
Paati had filled a big steel plate with small clay lamps. Each one had a little oil and a cotton wick.
"This year you two will do the front steps," Paati said. "I will do the kolam. Do not run with the lamps."
The house had six steps going down to the street. Nila stood on the top one and thought.
"I know," she said. "One lamp on the top step. Two on the next. Three on the next. All the way down."
"Why?" said Kannan.
"Because then it gets wider and wider, like a river of lights."
Kannan liked that. He put one lamp in the middle of the top step. Nila put two on the second step. Kannan put three on the third.
Then he ran back to the plate. "How many now?" he asked. "I have to count the steps again."
"You do not have to count anything," said Nila. "Last time was three. So now it is one more."
Kannan looked at his fingers. "Four?"
"Four."
He carried four lamps, two in each hand, walking like a very careful duck. Nila did the fifth step. Before she went to the plate she already knew she needed five.
"And the last step is mine," said Kannan. He did not ask how many. He stood still and thought. Then he took six.
Paati came with the long matchsticks and lit every lamp. The steps glowed, one, two, three, four, five, six, all the way down to the street.
"Now come and eat," said Paati.
They were halfway through the pori urundai when the wind came. It was a short, cold wind, the kind that comes before rain. The door banged. Out on the street, somebody shouted.
Nila and Kannan ran to the door. Most of the lamps were still burning. But it was dark now, and nobody could see the lamps themselves any more. They could only see the flames.
"Some went out," said Kannan. "I can feel it. It looks wrong."
"Which ones?" said Paati. She had the matchsticks ready. "I cannot go down feeling every lamp in the dark with my knees."
Kannan started to count all the flames from the top. "One, two, three, four, five..." He lost his place somewhere in the middle and began again.
Nila did not count them all. She looked at one step at a time.
"Top step, one flame. Good. Next step, two. Good. Next, three. Good." She stopped. "Next step, three."
"So?" said Kannan.
"So it cannot be three again. After three comes four. One lamp on the fourth step is out."
She went on. "Fifth step, five. Good. Last step..." She counted twice. "Four. It should be six. Two are out down there."
Paati looked at her for a moment. Then she went down slowly, holding the wall. On the fourth step she found one cold lamp at the end of the row. On the last step she found two.
She lit all three. The river of lights was whole again.
"How did you know where to look?" Paati asked, when she had climbed back up.
"The steps told me," said Nila. "Each one has to be one more than the one before. If it is not, something is missing there."
Kannan was looking down the steps with his head on one side.
"If we had a seventh step," he said, "it would need seven."
"We do not have a seventh step," said Paati.
"I know," said Kannan. "But it would."
Then the first drops of rain came, and all three of them ran to carry the lamps under the roof, six at a time.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a number pattern is more than a list. Once Nila knows the rule, one more each time, she knows how many lamps each step needs without counting from the top. The same rule shows her where something is wrong, because a step that breaks the rule stands out. And Kannan sees that the rule goes on past the steps that exist.
ask: How did Kannan know to take six lamps for the last step, without counting the steps?
The fourth step had three flames. How did Nila know that was wrong?
Kannan counted every flame from the top. Nila looked at one step at a time. Why was her way quicker?
There is no seventh step. How can Kannan know how many lamps it would need?
art: Two children on the top step of a house at dusk, a steel plate of small clay lamps between them, a grandmother drawing a kolam on the street below.
Six steps with lamps set out in rows of one, two, three, four, five and six, all lit, glowing down to the street.
The children in the doorway at night looking down at the flames, a gust of wind bending them, one gap visible on the fourth step.

experiments.title: The Staircase Test: can you know a step before you build it?
experiments.context: In this test you lay chana in rows that make a staircase. Before each new row you guess how many it will need, and say why. You will find out whether a pattern can tell you about a row nobody has built yet.
experiments.question: If we know the first few rows of a staircase, can we know a later row before we build it?
experiments.predict: Before each new row, guess: how many chana will it need? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We write the guess down before we build the row, so nobody can change it afterwards. We use chana that are all about the same size, and we line every row up on the left so the rows are easy to compare.
results_table: My guess for the next row

materials.item: chana, rajma or buttons, all about the same size
a newspaper sheet or a mat to work on, so nothing rolls away
paper and a pencil, for the table
a small towel or a strip of paper, to hide one row

experiments.safety: Keep chana, beans and buttons away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Build a staircase that grows by one, one that grows by two and one that shrinks by two. Guess each new row before building it. Then find a hidden row and a wrong row.

experiments.record: A grown-up draws the table. For each staircase, write the guess and what was built. At the end, the child says what they found, and the grown-up writes it under the table.

example_chart.title: What a finished table can look like (your guesses will be your own)

setup.art: Chana on a newspaper sheet laid in three rows of one, two and three, all lined up on the left, with a heap of spare chana beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay rows of 1, 2 and 3 chana, lined up on the left.

setup.art: A child holding up five fingers as a guess while a grown-up writes in a table, the fourth row just finished.
setup.caption: 2. Guess the next row and say why. Then build it.

setup.art: The staircase of six rows with a small towel folded over the fourth row, and a child pointing at the rows above and below.
setup.caption: 3. Hide one row. How many are under the towel?

flow.do: 1. Spread the newspaper. 2. Lay a row of 1 chana. Under it lay a row of 2, then a row of 3. 3. Line the rows up on the left. 4. Say nothing about the rule. Ask what your child notices.
flow.say: Look at my rows. What do you notice? What is happening from one row to the next?
flow.kid: Look at the rows of chana. What changes from one row to the next?

ask.q: What do you notice?

flow.parent: Take any answer. Do not say the rule yet. If your child says 'it gets bigger', ask 'by how much?'
flow.context: This is the first step of the Staircase Test. A grown-up lays rows of 1, 2 and 3 chana, and you say what you notice.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a guess for row 4, and the reason. Write the guess. 2. Your child builds row 4. 3. Do the same for row 5. 4. Now ask about row 7, without building row 6. Write the guess. 5. Build rows 6 and 7 to check.
flow.say: How many chana will the next row need? Why do you think so? Now, what about row 7?
flow.kid: Guess how many the next row needs. Say why. Then build it and check.

ask.q: Why did you guess that for row 7?
good: It goes one more each time: 6, then 7.
The row number is how many.

flow.parent: Row 7 is the real test, because row 6 is not there to look at. Some children guess 6. Let the building show it.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the Staircase Test. You guess how many chana rows 4, 5 and 7 need, and then build them.

flow.do: 1. Sweep the chana into a heap. 2. In a clear space lay rows of 2, 4 and 6. 3. Ask what is different this time. 4. Ask for a guess for the next row, and why. Write it. 5. Your child builds it. 6. Guess and build one more row.
flow.say: Here is a new staircase. What is different about it? How many will the next row need? Why?
flow.kid: This staircase is new. Guess the next row. Say why. Then build it.

ask.q: What is different about this staircase?
good: It is two more each time.

flow.parent: The next rows are 8 and 10. A guess of 7 means your child is still using the old rule, one more. Building the row and laying it under the 6 shows the gap.
flow.context: This is step 3 of the Staircase Test. A new staircase has rows of 2, 4 and 6 chana, and you guess the next two rows.

flow.do: 1. Sweep up again. 2. Lay a row of 9. Under it lay a row of 7, then a row of 5. 3. Ask what is happening now. 4. Ask for a guess for the next two rows, and why. Write the guesses. 5. Your child builds them.
flow.say: Now look at this one. What is happening? What will the next row be? And the one after?
flow.kid: Look at these rows. Are they growing? Guess the next two rows. Then build them.

ask.q: Can there be another row after the row of 1? Why?
good: No, you cannot take two from one.

flow.parent: The rows shrink by two: 9, 7, 5, 3, 1. A guess of 4 means one fewer, not two fewer. With chana the staircase must stop at 1.
flow.context: This is step 4 of the Staircase Test. The rows are 9, 7 and 5 chana long, and you guess the next two rows.

flow.do: 1. Your child closes their eyes. 2. Build the 'one more' staircase again, rows 1 to 6. 3. Cover row 4 with the towel. 4. Your child opens their eyes and says how many are hidden, and why. 5. Lift the towel to check. 6. Swap: your child hides a row for you.
flow.say: One row is hiding under the towel. How many chana are under it? How do you know?
flow.kid: One row is hiding. How many chana are in it? Say how you know. Then look.

ask.q: How did you know without looking?
good: The row before has 3 and the row after has 5.
It is the fourth row, so 4.

check.q: A staircase goes 1, 2, 3, then a hidden row, then 5. How many are in the hidden row?
check.why: 4. Each row is one more than the row before. One more than 3 is 4, and one more than 4 is 5, so it fits. Picking 3 or 5 means copying a row you can see.

flow.context: This is step 5 of the Staircase Test. One row of the 'one more' staircase is hidden under a towel, and you work out how many chana it has.

flow.do: 1. Your child closes their eyes again. 2. Lay rows of 2, 4, 5 and 8. 3. Ask your child to find the row that breaks the rule. 4. Your child fixes it.
flow.say: I have made a mistake in one row. Which row is wrong? How can you tell? Fix it for me.
flow.kid: One row is wrong. Find it. Say how you know. Then fix it.

ask.q: How did you find the wrong row?
good: It only went up by one there.
The step was not the same.

flow.parent: The row of 5 should be 6. Your child adds one chana to it. Then every step is two.
flow.context: This is step 6 of the Staircase Test. A staircase of 2, 4, 5 and 8 chana has one wrong row, and you find and fix it.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child what they think, what they saw, and why. 3. Write their words under the table.
flow.say: Look at your guesses. How could you know row 7 before it was built? What did you need to know?
flow.kid: Look at your table. How did you know a row before building it?

ask.q: What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it is so?
good: If you know the rule you can tell the next one.
It was one more every time, so row 7 was 7.
When the rule was two more, my old guess was wrong.
You need to know how much it changes each time.

check.q: A staircase has rows of 2, 4 and 6. What do you need to know to build the next row?
options: The rule: two more each time
check.why: The rule. Each row is two more than the last, so the next row is 8. Counting the rows gives 3, which does not tell you the next row here.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Staircase Test. You say what you found: how a pattern lets you know a row before you build it.

activities.title: Number Track: hop the pattern
activities.context: In this activity you make a number track from 0 to 20 and hop a button along it in equal jumps. You will see that a number pattern is equal hops along the track.
activities.problem: On a number track, 'two more each time' is a hop of two boxes. Where do the hops land?

materials.item: a long strip of paper, or two sheets taped end to end
a pencil or a sketch pen
a button to hop with
chana or rajma, to mark the boxes you land on

activities.safety: Keep chana, beans and buttons away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Make a number track from 0 to 20. Hop in twos from 0 and from 1. Then hop backwards.

activities.record: On paper, write the numbers you landed on for each pattern. Under each row, write the rule in words, such as 'two more each time'.

setup.art: A long paper strip ruled into 21 boxes with the numbers 0 to 20 written in them, and a button on the box marked 0.
setup.caption: 1. Draw 21 boxes in a row. Write 0 to 20.

setup.art: A button hopping over one box at a time along the strip, with a chana left on 2, 4 and 6.
setup.caption: 2. Hop two boxes each time. Leave a chana where you land.

setup.art: The same strip with a button near 20 and an arrow hopping backwards to 18 and 16.
setup.caption: 3. Start at 20 and hop backwards.

flow.do: 1. Rule 21 boxes in a row on the paper strip, each about two fingers wide. 2. Your child writes 0 to 20 in the boxes. 3. Put the button on 0.
flow.say: Let us make a track of numbers. Write 0 in the first box. What comes in the next box?
flow.kid: Draw 21 boxes in a row. Write 0 to 20 in them. Put a button on 0.
flow.parent: Help with the numbers from 11 to 20 if they are shaky. Saying them aloud together is enough.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Number Track activity. You make a strip of boxes numbered 0 to 20.

flow.do: 1. Your child hops the button two boxes at a time from 0. 2. They leave one chana on each box they land on. 3. Stop at 10 and ask where the next hop will land. 4. Go on to 20. 5. Read the chana numbers aloud.
flow.say: Hop two boxes each time. Put a chana where you land. Before you hop from 10, tell me where you will land.
flow.kid: Hop two boxes each time. Leave a chana where you land. Go to 20.

ask.q: Look at the chana. What do you notice about the boxes with no chana?
good: There is one empty box in each gap.

chart.title: Start on 0. Hop two boxes each time.

flow.context: This is step 2 of the Number Track activity, done on a strip of boxes numbered 0 to 20. Here you hop two boxes at a time from 0.

flow.do: 1. Leave the chana where they are. 2. Put the button on 1. 3. Ask: if you hop in twos from 1, will you land on any chana? Why? 4. Your child hops and finds out.
flow.say: Now start on 1. Same rule, two more each time. Will you ever land on a chana? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Start on 1 now. Hop two each time. Will you land on a chana? Guess, then hop.

ask.q: What numbers did you land on this time?
good: The ones I jumped over before.

flow.parent: From 1 the button lands on 1, 3, 5 and so on to 19, and never on a chana. The rule is the same and the start is different.

check.q: You start on 1 and hop two boxes each time. Which numbers do you land on?
check.why: From 1, two more is 3, then 5, then 7. Picking 2, 4, 6 means starting from 0. Picking 2, 3, 4 means hopping one box, not two.

chart.title: Start on 1. Hop two boxes each time.

flow.context: This is step 3 of the Number Track activity, done on a strip of boxes numbered 0 to 20. Here you hop two boxes at a time from 1.

flow.do: 1. Take the chana off. 2. Put the button on 20. 3. Your child hops back one box at a time for five hops, saying each number. 4. Then they hop back two boxes at a time from 20 to 10.
flow.say: Now we go backwards. Start on 20 and hop back one each time. Then try two each time.
flow.kid: Start on 20. Hop back one box each time. Then hop back two each time.

ask.q: You hopped back in twos from 20. What numbers did you say?
good: The same ones as going up, but backwards.

flow.parent: Backwards in ones: 19, 18, 17, 16, 15. Backwards in twos: 18, 16, 14, 12, 10. Hopping back in twos is hard at first. Let the track do the work.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Number Track activity, done on a strip of boxes numbered 0 to 20. Here you hop backwards to make shrinking patterns.

activities.title: Pattern Hunt: a book, the stairs and a countdown
activities.context: In this activity you look for number patterns in three things at home: the page numbers of a book, the stairs or floor tiles, and a countdown. You will find that number patterns are already all around you.
activities.problem: Where at home do numbers go up or down by the same step each time?

materials.item: any book with page numbers
stairs, or a row of floor tiles
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: On real stairs, a grown-up stays beside the child, and the child holds the rail. Use floor tiles if your home has no stairs.

schedule.what: Find the pattern in the right-hand pages of a book, in stairs taken two at a time, and in a countdown.

activities.record: Write the three patterns you found, one under the other. Beside each, write its rule.

setup.art: An open story book on a child's lap with the page numbers at the bottom corners circled in pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Turn the pages. Read only the right-hand page numbers.

setup.art: A child standing on the second tile of a row of floor tiles, each tile with a chalk number, about to step over one tile.
setup.caption: 2. Number the stairs or tiles. Step over one each time.

setup.art: A child crouching with five fingers up, counting down before jumping.
setup.caption: 3. Count down from 10 and jump at zero.

flow.do: 1. Open the book near the start. 2. Your child reads the number on the right-hand page. 3. Turn one leaf and read the right-hand page again. 4. After three numbers, ask for a guess for the next one. 5. Write the numbers down.
flow.say: Read me the number on this side only. Turn the page. And now? What will the next one be? Why?
flow.kid: Read the right-hand page number. Turn the page. Read again. Guess the next one.

ask.q: What is the rule for the right-hand pages?
good: The skipped number is on the back.

flow.parent: In most books the right-hand pages go 1, 3, 5, 7. Each leaf has two sides, so the number jumps by two.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Pattern Hunt. You read only the right-hand page numbers of a book and look for the rule.

flow.do: 1. Chalk the numbers 1 to 10 on ten stairs or ten floor tiles in a row. 2. Your child starts before number 1 and steps over one each time. 3. They say each number they land on.
flow.say: Step over one each time. Tell me the numbers you land on. Which ones did you step over?
flow.kid: Step over one stair or tile each time. Say the numbers you land on.

ask.q: Which numbers did you land on?

flow.parent: On real stairs, stay beside your child and have them hold the rail. Tiles on the floor work just as well.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the Pattern Hunt. You walk a row of ten numbered stairs or tiles, stepping over one each time.

flow.do: 1. Your child crouches down. 2. Count down together from 10 to 0, one number each second. 3. At zero your child jumps up. 4. Ask what the rule was. 5. Do it again from 10 in twos.
flow.say: Let us count down from 10. Jump at zero. What was the rule? Now let us count down in twos.
flow.kid: Crouch down. Count back from 10 to 0. Jump at zero!

ask.q: Which countdown had fewer numbers to say? Why?

check.q: A countdown goes 10, 8, 6. What is the rule?
check.why: Two fewer each time. From 10 down to 8 is two, and from 8 down to 6 is two. Picking 'two more' has the right step but the wrong way: the numbers are getting smaller.

flow.parent: In twos the countdown is 10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 0. It has six numbers. In ones it has eleven.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Pattern Hunt. You count down from 10 to zero, first in ones and then in twos.

activities.title: Maths in life: the dots of a 7 to 1 kolam
activities.context: In this activity you put down the dots for a kolam, a pattern drawn on the ground with rice flour. Many kolams start from rows of dots that shrink by the same number each time. You will lay the dots by following a number rule.
activities.problem: People who draw kolams often name a dot pattern by its numbers, such as '7 to 1'. What do the numbers tell them to do?

materials.item: chalk or rice flour on the floor, or a pencil and paper
someone at home or next door who draws kolams, if you can ask them

schedule.what: Put down a middle row of 7 dots. Add rows of 5, 3 and 1 above and below. Count the dots and join them in your own way.

activities.record: Keep your paper, or take a photo of the floor. Beside each row, write how many dots it has.

setup.art: A hand putting down a row of seven chalk dots on a swept floor, a hand-width apart.
setup.caption: 1. Put 7 dots in a row. This is the middle row.

setup.art: The row of seven dots with a row of five dots above it, each dot straight above a dot below, with the two end dots left out.
setup.caption: 2. Above it, put a row of 5. Leave out one dot at each end.

setup.art: A full diamond of dots with rows of 1, 3, 5, 7, 5, 3 and 1.
setup.caption: 3. Go on to 3 and 1. Do the same below.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts down 7 dots in a straight row, about a hand-width apart. 2. Say that the next row goes above it, with one dot left out at each end. 3. Ask how many dots that row will have, before putting any down.
flow.say: Here is the middle row of 7. The next row leaves out one dot at each end. How many dots will it have? Why?
flow.kid: Put 7 dots in a row. The next row drops one dot at each end. How many dots?

ask.q: One dot fewer at each end. How many fewer is that in all?

flow.parent: The next row has 5 dots. One left out at each end makes two fewer in all.
flow.context: This is the first step of the 7 to 1 kolam. You put down a middle row of 7 dots and guess the next row.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts the row of 5 above the 7, each dot straight above a dot below. 2. Ask for the next row, and the next. 3. Your child puts down the rows of 3 and 1.
flow.say: After 7 came 5. What comes after 5? And then? Put them down.
flow.kid: Put a row of 5 above the 7. What comes next? Put those rows down too.

ask.q: Why is this kolam called '7 to 1'?
good: It starts at 7 and goes down to 1.

check.q: The rows of dots go 7, 5, 3. How many dots are in the next row?
check.why: 1. The rule is two fewer each time, and two fewer than 3 is 1. Picking 2 means taking away only one.

flow.context: This is step 2 of the 7 to 1 kolam. Above a row of 7 dots you add rows that shrink by two each time.

flow.do: 1. Your child does the same below the middle row: 5, then 3, then 1. 2. Read the rows from top to bottom together. 3. Ask where the pattern grows and where it shrinks.
flow.say: Now the same below. Read me all the rows from the top. Where does it grow? Where does it shrink?
flow.kid: Put rows of 5, 3 and 1 below the 7. Read all the rows from the top.

ask.q: Read the rows from the top. What do you notice?
good: It is the same from the top and from the bottom.

flow.parent: From the top the rows go 1, 3, 5, 7, 5, 3, 1. They grow by two up to the middle, then shrink by two.
flow.context: This is step 3 of the 7 to 1 kolam. You add rows of dots below the middle row and read the whole pattern.

chart.title: All the rows of a 7 to 1 kolam

flow.do: 1. Your child joins the dots in any way they like, or loops a line around them. 2. If someone nearby draws kolams, ask them to show a '7 to 1' kolam, or one with other numbers. 3. Ask how they remember where the dots go.
flow.say: Now make it yours. Join the dots or loop around them. Let us ask how a kolam is remembered.
flow.kid: Join the dots your own way. Ask someone how they remember a kolam.
flow.parent: Many people remember a kolam by its dot numbers alone. Other kolams are '5 to 1' or '9 to 1'. Some use rows that shrink by one, with the dots set in the gaps of the row below.
flow.context: This is the last step of the 7 to 1 kolam. You finish your own kolam and ask someone how they remember the dots.

activities.title: Maths in life: a chant that grows and shrinks
activities.context: In this activity you say and clap a chant that gets one beat longer each time, and then one beat shorter. South Indian musicians build growing and shrinking patterns like this into songs and drumming. You will hear a number pattern with your ears.
activities.problem: Can a pattern grow in sound, the way a staircase grows in chana?

materials.item: your hands and your voice
chana, to lay a row for each line of the chant

activities.safety: Keep chana, beans and buttons away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Learn the growing chant, lay it out in chana, then say it backwards so that it shrinks.

activities.record: Draw a dot for each beat of each line, one line under the other. Your drawing should look like a staircase.

setup.art: A parent and child sitting facing each other, the parent clapping once with the word 'ta' written above.
setup.caption: 1. Say 'ta' with one clap. Then 'ta ka' with two.

setup.art: A child clapping while chana lie on the floor in rows of one, two, three and four.
setup.caption: 2. Go on to three and four. Lay one chana for each clap.

setup.art: The same rows of chana with an arrow pointing back up from the row of four to the row of one.
setup.caption: 3. Now say it backwards: four, three, two, one.

flow.do: 1. Sit facing your child. 2. Say each line slowly with one clap for each sound. Line 1: ta. Line 2: ta ka. Line 3: ta ki ta. Line 4: ta ka di mi. 3. Your child copies each line after you.
flow.say: Listen and copy me. Ta. Ta ka. Ta ki ta. Ta ka di mi. How many claps was each line?
flow.kid: Say and clap each line. Ta. Ta ka. Ta ki ta. Ta ka di mi.

ask.q: How many claps were in each line?

flow.parent: These sounds are real. South Indian drummers and dancers use them to say rhythms aloud. One clap for each sound is all that matters here.
flow.context: This is the first step of the growing chant. You say and clap four lines, each one sound longer than the last.

flow.do: 1. Say the chant again. 2. This time your child lays one chana for each clap, a new row for each line. 3. Ask what the rows look like.
flow.say: Say it again, and put down one chana for each clap. Start a new row for each line. What does it look like?
flow.kid: Say the chant again. Put one chana for each clap. Start a new row each line.

ask.q: What do the rows of chana look like?
good: The same as the Staircase Test.

flow.context: This is step 2 of the growing chant, four lines of 1, 2, 3 and 4 claps. Here you lay one chana for each clap.

flow.do: 1. Now say the lines from the longest to the shortest: four claps, three, two, one. 2. Then say the whole thing up and down without stopping. 3. Ask whether the pattern is growing, shrinking or repeating.
flow.say: Now backwards. Ta ka di mi. Ta ki ta. Ta ka. Ta. Is that growing or shrinking? What is the rule?
flow.kid: Now start with the long line. End with one clap. Is it growing or shrinking?

ask.q: What is the rule when we say it backwards?

check.q: You clap 1 time, then 2 times, then 3 times. How many claps come next?
check.why: 4. It is a growing pattern, one more each time. Picking 1 means thinking the pattern starts again, as a repeating pattern would.

flow.parent: A famous song does the same with words. In 'Tyagaraja Yoga Vaibhavam' by Muthuswami Dikshitar, the first line is sung again and again, a little shorter each time, until only 'vam' is left. Musicians call this shape gopuccha, the cow's tail. Later in the song a line grows instead.
flow.context: This is the last step of the growing chant. You say the four lines from longest to shortest, so the pattern shrinks.

activities.title: Everyone does maths: read a tree's rings
activities.context: In this activity you draw how a teak tree's trunk grows, one ring each year, and then count the rings in a piece of real wood. A tree is another living being who builds a pattern one step at a time.
activities.problem: A teak tree usually adds one ring of wood each year. How can the rings tell you how old the tree was?

materials.item: paper and a pencil or crayons
a piece of wood that shows rings, if you can find one: the cut end of a log, a tree stump or a wooden chopping board

schedule.what: Draw a tree trunk growing ring by ring for five years. Then count the rings in a piece of real wood.

activities.record: Keep your drawing of the five trunks. Under each one, write the tree's age.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a small circle drawn on it, labelled 'year 1'.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a small circle. The tree is 1 year old.

setup.art: Five drawings in a row: a circle, then two circles one inside the other, then three, four and five, each labelled with a year.
setup.caption: 2. Each year, draw the trunk again with one more ring around it.

setup.art: A child's finger counting the rings on the cut end of a log from the centre outwards.
setup.caption: 3. Find real wood. Count the rings from the middle out.

flow.do: 1. Draw a small circle and say this is a baby teak's trunk after one year. 2. Beside it your child draws the trunk after two years: the small circle with a bigger ring around it. 3. Ask how many rings the next drawing will have.
flow.say: This is a teak's trunk after one year. Each year they grow one more ring. Draw year 2. How many rings in year 3?
flow.kid: Draw the trunk for year 2. Add one ring around the first. How many for year 3?

ask.q: How many rings will the tree have after 3 years?

flow.context: This is the first step of reading a tree's rings. You draw a teak trunk growing one ring each year.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws years 3, 4 and 5. 2. Draw a new trunk with 8 rings, without saying the number. 3. Ask how old this tree is, and how many rings they will have next year.
flow.say: Here is another tree. How old are they? How many rings will they have next year?
flow.kid: Draw years 3, 4 and 5. Then count the rings on the new tree. How old are they?

ask.q: How old is the tree with 8 rings? And next year?

check.q: A teak has 6 rings this year. How many rings will the tree have next year?
check.why: 7. A teak adds about one ring each year, and one more than 6 is 7. Picking 5 means counting back, not on.

flow.parent: Count from the middle outwards, and touch each ring once.
flow.context: This is step 2 of reading a tree's rings. You count the rings in a drawing to find a tree's age.

flow.do: 1. Find a piece of wood that shows rings. 2. Your child counts the rings from the middle outwards. 3. Ask whether all the rings are the same width. 4. If you have no wood, look at the lines on a wooden door or table and talk about what they might be.
flow.say: Count the rings from the middle out. Are they all the same width? What could make one year's ring wider?
flow.kid: Find wood with rings. Count them from the middle out. Are they all the same width?

ask.q: Why might one ring be wider than another?

flow.parent: Rings are usually wider in years with good rain. Not every kind of tree makes clear yearly rings. Teak does. A chopping board cut along the trunk shows the rings as long lines, not circles.
flow.context: This is the last step of reading a tree's rings. You count the rings in a piece of real wood and look at how wide they are.

games.title: What Is My Rule?
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a guessing game with rule cards and a number track. One player secretly follows a rule and hops a button along the track. The others watch the hops and say the rule and the next number. It builds quick finding of rules.
rules: You need the number track from 0 to 20, a button and 10 chana for scoring. To make a track, draw 21 boxes in a row and write 0 to 20 in them.
Shuffle the rule cards and the start cards. Put them in two piles, face down.
On your turn you are the maker. Take one rule card and one start card. Look at them secretly.
Put the button on your start number. Hop it three times by your rule, saying nothing.
The other players say the next number, and then the rule. The first to get both right takes one chana.
If nobody is right, the maker hops once more and they try again.
The maker passes to the next player. The first player with 3 chana wins.
Playing alone: turn over one card from each pile. Say the first five numbers aloud. Then check by hopping the button.

setup.art: A number track from 0 to 20 on a table, two small piles of face-down cards, a button and a little heap of chana.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the track. Shuffle the two piles of cards.

setup.art: A child peeking at two cards held close to her chest, one reading 'Two fewer each time' and one reading 'Start at 12'.
setup.caption: 2. The maker takes one rule and one start, in secret.

setup.art: A button on the track at 8 with small arcs showing it came from 12 and 10, and another child pointing at 6.
setup.caption: 3. Watch three hops. Say the next number and the rule.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards, or write them on slips of paper. 2. Lay out the number track. 3. Shuffle the two piles and put them face down. 4. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: One of us will follow a secret rule. The others must work out the rule from the hops.
flow.kid: Lay out the track. Shuffle the cards. Put them face down in two piles.

chart.title: The board for What Is My Rule?

flow.context: This is the first step of What Is My Rule?, a guessing game on a number track from 0 to 20. Here you set up.

flow.do: 1. Play one practice turn as the maker, with your cards face up. 2. Say the start, hop three times and say each number. 3. Ask for the next number, then the rule.
flow.say: My cards say start at 12, two fewer each time. Watch: 12, 10, 8, 6. What comes next? What is my rule?
flow.kid: Watch the button hop. Say the next number. Then say the rule.

check.q: The button starts on 12 and hops to 10, then 8, then 6. What is the rule?
check.why: Two fewer each time. Each hop goes back two boxes. Picking 'one fewer' has the right way but the wrong size of step. Count the boxes in one hop.

chart.title: Start at 12. Where does it hop?

flow.context: This is step 2 of What Is My Rule?, a guessing game on a number track from 0 to 20. Here you practise one turn with the cards face up.

flow.do: 1. Play the game, taking turns as the maker. 2. Each time, the guessers say the next number first and then the rule. 3. Now and then, ask a guesser how they knew.
flow.say: Your turn to be the maker. Keep your cards secret. We will watch your hops.
flow.kid: Take turns as the maker. Hop three times in secret. The others guess.

ask.q: How did you know the rule so fast?
good: I counted the boxes in one hop.
The gap was two each time.

flow.parent: Every start card works with every rule card. The button can never run off the track in four hops.
flow.context: This is step 3 of What Is My Rule?, a guessing game on a number track from 0 to 20. Here you play.

flow.do: 1. When someone has 3 chana, the game ends. 2. Ask which rule was the hardest to spot, and why.
flow.say: Who has three? Which rule was the hardest to spot?
flow.kid: The first to 3 chana wins. Which rule was the hardest to spot?
flow.context: This is the last step of What Is My Rule?, a guessing game on a number track from 0 to 20. Here you finish and talk about the rules.

games.title: Fill the Gap
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a card game. Each card shows a number pattern with one number missing. The answer and the rule are on the back. It builds quick finding of missing numbers.

printables.title: 16 gap cards to cut out, with the answer on the back

rules: Shuffle the 16 cards. Put them in a pile with the gap side up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say the missing number and the rule.
Turn the card over to check. If both are right, keep the card.
If you were wrong, put the card at the bottom of the pile.
Then it is the next player's turn.
When the pile is gone, the player with the most cards wins.
Playing alone: go through the pile once. Make a 'got it' pile and a 'try again' pile. Then go through the 'try again' pile until it is empty.
A harder game: before you turn the card over, also say the number that would come after the last one.

setup.art: Sixteen small paper cards in a pile on a table, the top one reading '2, 4, __, 8'.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the cards. Gap side up.

setup.art: A child holding a card that reads '9, 8, __, 6' and saying '7, one fewer each time'.
setup.caption: 2. Say the missing number and the rule.

setup.art: The same card turned over to show '7. One fewer each time.' and the child adding it to her own small pile.
setup.caption: 3. Turn it over to check. Right? Keep it.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards, or copy them on slips of paper with the answers on the back. 2. Shuffle them. 3. Put them in a pile, gap side up. 4. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: Each card has a pattern with a gap. Say what is missing and what the rule is.
flow.kid: Shuffle the cards. Put them in a pile with the gap side up.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fill the Gap, a card game about patterns with one number missing. Here you set up.

flow.do: 1. Take one practice turn each. 2. Read the card aloud and say 'gap' for the missing number. 3. Find the rule from two numbers side by side. 4. Say the missing number, then turn over.
flow.say: My card says 9, 8, gap, 6. From 9 to 8 is one fewer. So the gap is 7. I turn over to check.
flow.kid: Read your card aloud. Find the rule. Say the missing number. Turn over.

check.q: A card says 10, 8, gap, 4. What is the missing number?
check.why: 6. From 10 to 8 is two fewer. Two fewer than 8 is 6, and two fewer than 6 is 4, so it fits. Picking 7 means going down by one.

flow.parent: If the gap is at the start, find the rule from the numbers after it, then go one step the other way.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Fill the Gap, a card game about patterns with one number missing. Here you practise one turn.

flow.do: 1. Play through the pile. 2. Each player says the missing number and the rule before turning over. 3. Wrong cards go to the bottom.
flow.say: Your turn. Read it out. What is missing? What is the rule?
flow.kid: Play the game. Say the missing number and the rule each time.

ask.q: The gap was the first number. How did you find it?
good: I found the rule from the others.
I tried a number and checked.

flow.context: This is step 3 of Fill the Gap, a card game about patterns with one number missing. Here you play.

flow.do: 1. When the pile is gone, count the cards. 2. Ask each player to make up one gap card for someone else.
flow.say: Count your cards. Now make up a gap pattern for me to solve.
flow.kid: Count your cards. Then make up a gap pattern for someone else.
flow.context: This is the last step of Fill the Gap, a card game about patterns with one number missing. Here you count up and invent a card.

projects.title: The One-More Jar: five days
projects.context: In this five-day project you put chana in a jar: 1 on the first day, 2 on the second, and one more each day. Each day you guess tomorrow's number. On the last day you find out how many are in the jar altogether.
projects.problem: If you add one more than yesterday each day, how fast does a jar fill?

materials.item: a clean jar or a steel tumbler
chana, rajma or one-rupee coins
a sheet of paper and a pencil

projects.safety: Keep chana, beans and buttons away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Put 1 chana in the jar. Draw 1 dot on the paper. Guess tomorrow's number.
Put in 2 chana. Draw a row of 2 dots under yesterday's row. Guess tomorrow's number.
Put in 3 chana and draw a row of 3 dots. Guess how many are in the jar altogether, then tip them out and count.
Put in 4 chana and draw the row. Guess the total again before counting.
Put in 5 chana and draw the row. Guess the total, count, and say what days 6 and 7 would need.

projects.record: The sheet of paper is the record. Each day has one row of dots, and the rows make a staircase. Beside each row, write the day's number and the total in the jar.

setup.caption: 1. Day 1: one chana in the jar, one dot on the paper.

setup.art: The same jar with a few more chana, and the paper showing rows of one, two and three dots.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, one more than yesterday. Draw the row.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts 1 chana in the jar and draws 1 dot at the top of the paper. 2. Say that each day gets one more than the day before. 3. Ask for tomorrow's number and write the guess.
flow.say: Today the jar gets 1. Each day it gets one more than the day before. How many will it get tomorrow?
flow.kid: Put 1 chana in the jar. Draw 1 dot. How many go in tomorrow?
flow.context: This is day 1 of the One-More Jar, a five-day project. Each day you put in one more chana than the day before.

flow.do: 1. On days 2, 3 and 4, your child puts in that day's number and draws that day's row. 2. From day 3, ask for a guess of the total in the jar before counting. 3. Tip the chana out, count them, and put them back. 4. Write the total beside the row.
flow.say: What is today's number? Put them in. Now guess: how many are in the jar altogether? Tip them out and count.
flow.kid: Put in today's number. Draw the row. Guess the total. Then tip them out and count.

ask.q: Is the total going up by the same amount each day?
good: No, it goes up by more each day.
First 2 more, then 3 more, then 4 more.

flow.parent: The totals are 1, 3, 6 and 10. The day's number grows by one. The total grows by a bigger step each day.
flow.wait: Do this on each of the next three days.
flow.context: These are days 2 to 4 of the One-More Jar, a five-day project. Each day you put in one more chana than the day before, and count the total.

flow.do: 1. On day 5, your child puts in 5 chana and draws the row. 2. Ask for a guess of the total, then count. 3. Ask what days 6 and 7 would need. 4. Look at the staircase of dots together.
flow.say: Last day. How many today? How many in the jar now? What would day 6 need? And day 7?
flow.kid: Put in 5 chana. Guess the total, then count. What would day 6 need?

ask.q: On which day did the jar get the most? Was any day a big jump from the day before?
good: No, each day was only one more.

check.q: A jar gets 1 chana on day 1, 2 on day 2 and 3 on day 3. How many does it get on day 6?
check.why: 6. Each day gets one more than the day before, so the day's number is the same as the day. Picking 4 gives the very next day, not day 6.

flow.parent: After day 5 the jar holds 15: that is 1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and 5. Days 6 and 7 would need 6 and 7.
flow.context: This is day 5 of the One-More Jar, a five-day project. Today you count the whole jar and say what later days would need.

challenges.title: Stretch: how many chana make the whole staircase?
challenges.context: This is a puzzle that goes past Class 1. You have 20 chana. You build 'one more' staircases and find which ones use up their chana exactly. The point is to meet a pattern whose step grows.
challenges.problem: A staircase has rows of 1, 2, 3 and so on. How many chana does a staircase of 4 rows use altogether? And 5 rows? Find a quick way to know the next total without counting every chana again.
constraints: Every staircase starts with a row of 1 and grows by one each row.
You must say the total for the next staircase before you build it.
materials: a newspaper sheet or mat to work on
general: Build each staircase and count every chana from 1.
Keep the last total and count on for the new row.
Write the totals in a row and look for the rule between them.
creative: Build two staircases of the same size and fit them together. They make a block of equal rows that is easy to count. Half of the block is one staircase.
Look at the steps between the totals: 2, 3, 4, 5. The step is the number of the new row.
Draw the staircases on squared paper and colour each new row in a new colour.
challenges.your_turn: Now find your own quick way to get the next total. Use it to say how many chana a staircase of 6 rows needs. You do not have enough chana to build it, so explain how you know.

setup.art: Twenty chana in a heap on a newspaper sheet beside a small staircase of rows of one, two and three.
setup.caption: 1. Build rows of 1, 2 and 3. Count all the chana.

setup.art: Staircases of two, three and four rows side by side with their totals 3, 6 and 10 written below.
setup.caption: 2. Add a row. Write the new total each time.

setup.art: Two staircases of four rows fitted together into a block of four rows of five chana.
setup.caption: 3. One idea: fit two staircases together.

flow.do: 1. Your child builds a staircase of 3 rows: 1, 2, 3. 2. They count all the chana. 3. They add a row of 4 and count again. 4. Write the totals: 1 row, 2 rows, 3 rows, 4 rows.
flow.say: Build a staircase of three rows. How many chana in all? Add the next row. How many now?
flow.kid: Build rows of 1, 2 and 3. Count all the chana. Add a row of 4. Count again.
flow.parent: The totals are 1, then 3, then 6, then 10.
flow.context: This is the first step of the whole staircase puzzle. You build staircases of chana and write how many each one uses in all.

flow.do: 1. Point at the totals 1, 3, 6, 10. 2. Ask whether this is a 'one more' or a 'two more' pattern. 3. Ask how big each step is. 4. Ask for a guess for a staircase of 5 rows. Write it. 5. Your child builds it to check.
flow.say: Look at the totals: 1, 3, 6, 10. Is the step the same each time? What will the total be with 5 rows? Why?
flow.kid: Look at 1, 3, 6, 10. Is the step the same each time? Guess the next total.

ask.q: How big is each step between the totals?
good: It gets one bigger each time.
It is the same as the new row.

check.q: The totals go 1, 3, 6, 10. What comes next?
check.why: 15. The steps are 2, then 3, then 4, so the next step is 5. Five more than 10 is 15. Picking 12 means using a step of two every time.

flow.parent: A staircase of 5 rows uses 15 chana. The step between totals is the size of the new row.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the whole staircase puzzle, where the totals so far are 1, 3, 6 and 10. Here you look at the steps between the totals.

flow.do: 1. Ask: with 20 chana, can you build a staircase that uses every chana? 2. Your child tries. 3. Then show one creative idea if they want it: build two staircases of 3 rows and fit them into a block.
flow.say: You have 20 chana. Can you make a staircase with none left over? Try it.
flow.kid: Use all 20 chana in one staircase. Can it be done? Try.

ask.q: What happened with 20?
good: 5 rows uses 15 and there are 5 left.
The next row needs 6 and I only have 5.

flow.parent: It cannot be done. Five rows use 15, and the sixth row needs 6 more, which makes 21. Two staircases of 3 rows fit into a block of 3 rows of 4, which is 12. Half of 12 is 6.
flow.context: This is step 3 of the whole staircase puzzle. You try to build a staircase that uses exactly 20 chana.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say how many a staircase of 6 rows needs, and how they know. 2. Write their way of working it out. 3. Ask what a staircase of 7 rows would need.
flow.say: You cannot build 6 rows with 20 chana. So tell me: how many would it need? How do you know?
flow.kid: How many chana for 6 rows? You cannot build it. Say how you know.

ask.q: How many for 6 rows? And for 7?

flow.parent: Six rows need 21. Seven rows need 28. Any way of explaining that uses the growing step is a good one.
flow.context: This is the last step of the whole staircase puzzle. You work out the total for a staircase you do not have enough chana to build.

items.p: Look at the rows of dots. How many dots will the next row have?
items.why: 4. Each row has one more dot than the row above. One more than 3 is 4.

items.p: What comes next? 6, 7, 8, ____
items.why: The rule is one more each time. One more than 8 is 9.

items.p: What comes next? 2, 4, 6, ____
items.why: The rule is two more each time. Two more than 6 is 8.

items.p: What comes next in this pattern?
items.why: 7. The numbers go down by one each time. One fewer than 8 is 7. Picking 9 means going up, not down.

items.p: In 1, 2, 3, 4 the rule is one more each time.
items.why: True. From 1 to 2 is one more. So is 2 to 3, and 3 to 4.

items.p: What is the rule of the pattern 5, 7, 9?
items.why: Two more each time. On the number track, 5 to 7 is two hops, and 7 to 9 is two hops.

items.p: What is missing? 4, 5, ____, 7
items.why: The rule is one more each time. One more than 5 is 6, and one more than 6 is 7, so 6 fits.

items.p: Sort each pattern: is it growing or shrinking?
items.why: In a growing pattern each number is bigger than the one before. In a shrinking pattern each number is smaller.

items.p: Match each pattern to its rule.
items.why: Look at two numbers side by side. Ask whether it went up or down, and by how much.

items.p: Draw a staircase of dots with rows of 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.
items.a: Five rows of dots, lined up on the left. Each row has one more dot than the row above.
items.why: A strong drawing keeps the rule in every row. To check, count each row: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

items.p: The first two rows have 2 dots and 4 dots. Draw the next two rows.
items.a: A row of 6 dots, then a row of 8 dots.
items.why: The rule is two more each time. Two more than 4 is 6, and two more than 6 is 8.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. In the Staircase Test, how did you know row 7 before you built it?
items.a: Each row was one more than the row before. So row 7 had to have 7.
items.why: A strong answer names the rule, one more each time, and uses it to reach row 7.

worksheets.title: Up, Down and the Missing One (stretch)

items.p: What comes next? 11, 13, 15, ____
items.why: The rule is two more each time. Two more than 15 is 17.

items.p: Look at the pattern. What comes next? ____
items.why: The rule is two fewer each time. Two fewer than 14 is 12.

items.p: Which number is missing from this pattern?
items.why: 7. From 5 to 3 is two fewer, so the rule is two fewer. Two fewer than 9 is 7, and two fewer than 7 is 5. Picking 8 means going down by one.

items.p: This staircase should grow by two each time. Which row is wrong?
items.why: Row 3. It has 5 dots. Two more than 4 is 6, so it needs one more dot. Then 6 and two more is 8, which fits row 4.

items.p: Start at 1 and go up in twos. You will land on 6.
items.why: False. From 1 you land on 3, 5, 7. You jump over 6.

chart.title: Start on 1. Hop two each time.

items.p: Put these numbers in order to make a pattern that grows by two.
items.why: Start with the smallest, 3. Two more is 5. Two more is 7. Two more is 9.

items.p: Match each start and rule to the pattern it makes.
items.why: Say the start. Then use the rule three times to get the next three numbers.

items.p: A staircase has rows of 1, 2, 3, 4 chana. Row 9 has ____ chana.
items.why: Each row is one more than the last, starting from 1. So the row number tells how many. Row 9 has 9.

items.p: A button is on 7. It hops two more, three times. Where does it land?
items.why: 13. The hops land on 9, then 11, then 13. Picking 10 means hopping one box each time.

items.p: Draw the dots of a '5 to 1' kolam: rows of 5, 3 and 1 dots.
items.a: A row of 5 dots, a row of 3 above it and 1 dot on top. Each row leaves out one dot at each end.
items.why: The rule is two fewer each time. A strong drawing keeps the rows centred, one above the other.

items.p: Make up your own number pattern. Write its first five numbers. Then say its rule.
items.a: Any five numbers that go up or down by the same step each time, with the rule said in words.
items.why: A strong pattern keeps the same step all the way. Someone else should be able to say the sixth number.

items.p: A pattern begins 2, 4. What comes next?

views.says: 6. The rule is two more each time.
8. Each number is added to itself: 2 and 2, then 4 and 4.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other child has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, then says what the other child has right.
items.why: Both rules fit the two numbers you can see. Two more each time is the simplest rule, so 6 is the usual answer. A third number would settle it.

items.p: This pattern goes up by two. What is the first number? ____, 5, 7, 9
items.why: Go one step backwards. Two fewer than 5 is 3. Check: 3 and two more is 5.

items.p: Three cousins are each two years apart. The youngest is 6. How old is the oldest?
items.why: 10. The ages go 6, 8, 10. Picking 8 gives the middle cousin.

items.p: Carry on the pattern 12, 10, 8. It will land on 0.
Carry on the pattern 9, 7, 5. It will land on 0.
items.why: False. It goes 9, 7, 5, 3, 1. From 1 you cannot take away two chana, so it stops at 1.

items.p: This goes past Class 1. The dots show how many in all. What comes next?
items.why: 15. The steps are 2, then 3, then 4. The next step is 5, and five more than 10 is 15.

items.p: This goes past Class 1. What comes next? 5, 10, 15, ____
items.why: The rule is five more each time, like counting the fingers on one hand after another. Five more than 15 is 20.

items.p: Sort each one: does it grow, shrink or repeat?
items.why: A growing pattern gets bigger by a step each time. A shrinking pattern gets smaller. A repeating pattern has a part that comes again and again.

items.p: Which pattern has a wrong number in it?
items.why: 12, 10, 9, 6. It goes down by two, then by one, then by three. With two fewer each time it would be 12, 10, 8, 6.

items.p: A lift goes down two floors at a time. It stops at 9, 7, 5 and then ____.
items.why: The rule is two fewer each time. Two fewer than 5 is 3.

items.p: Draw a staircase of four rows that starts with 1 dot and grows by two.
items.why: Two more than 1 is 3. Two more than 3 is 5. Two more than 5 is 7.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A teak has 12 rings. How many rings 3 years from now? How do you know?
items.a: 15 rings. A teak adds about one ring each year: 13, 14, 15.
items.why: A strong answer uses the rule, one more each year, and counts on three times from 12.

items.p: A teak tree adds one ring every year. Is the tree doing maths?

views.says: Yes. The tree keeps a number pattern, one more each year.
No. The tree just grows. People are the ones who count the rings.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other child has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, then says what the other child has right.
items.why: People do not agree on this. The tree does build the pattern in their own body, step by step. It is also true that the counting and the number words are ours.

quiz.p: What comes next in this number pattern?
quiz.why: 10. The rule is one more each time. One more than 9 is 10.

quiz.p: Look at the rows of dots: 4, 6, 8. The next row has ____ dots.
quiz.why: The rule is two more each time. Two more than 8 is 10.
12. The numbers go down by one each time. One fewer than 13 is 12.
The rule is two fewer each time. Two fewer than 12 is 10.

quiz.p: What is the rule of the pattern 3, 5, 7, 9?
quiz.why: Two more each time. From 3 to 5 is two hops on the number track, and so is every other step. Picking 'three more' often comes from reading the first number, 3, as the rule.

quiz.p: Which pattern follows the rule 'one fewer each time'?
quiz.why: 9, 8, 7. Each number is one fewer than the one before. 5, 6, 7 goes up. 8, 6, 4 goes down by two.
From 10 to 11 is one more, so the rule is one more. One more than 8 is 9.

quiz.p: This staircase should grow by two each time. Which row has the wrong number of dots?
quiz.why: The row of 7. Two more than 4 is 6, so that row should have 6 dots. Then two more than 6 is 8, which fits.

quiz.p: Which rule built this staircase of dots?
quiz.why: Two more each time. The rows have 1, 3 and 5 dots. Each row is two longer than the row above.

quiz.p: A button starts on 4. It hops two more, two times. Where does it land?
quiz.why: 8. The first hop lands on 6 and the second on 8. Picking 6 means making only one hop.

quiz.p: You clap once, then twice, then three times, then four times. What kind of pattern is it?
quiz.why: Growing. Each turn has one clap more than the turn before. Nothing comes round again the same, so it is not a repeating pattern.
False. The part 1, 2 comes again and again. It is a repeating pattern. A growing pattern would go on to 3.

applications: A person saving money puts the same amount in a box each week. The total grows in equal steps.
A builder makes every stair the same height. People would trip if the step changed.
A calendar counts the days of a month: one more each day.
Before a rocket leaves Sriharikota, the countdown goes one fewer each second.
A person knitting a cap makes each round a few stitches smaller, so that the top closes.
A kolam is laid out with rows of dots that grow and shrink by the same number each time.
A bus conductor's tickets are numbered one more each time, so a missing ticket shows up.
Scientists count the rings of a teak tree, one for each year, to find out how old the wood is.

open_questions.q: Do other animals notice a rule like 'one more each time'?
open_questions.why_open: Tests show that some animals keep track of small numbers. Whether any of them notice that a row of numbers follows a rule is much harder to test, and nobody knows yet.

open_questions.q: How does a teak tree keep time?
open_questions.why_open: A teak's rings follow the wet and dry seasons. Scientists are still working out what happens inside the tree to start and stop the growing each year.

open_questions.q: Is there a simple rule for the numbers 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13?
open_questions.why_open: These are the numbers that cannot be shared out into equal groups, except in ones. They are called prime numbers. People have looked for more than two thousand years, and nobody has found a simple rule that gives the next one.

open_questions.q: Why does a plain rule like 'the same step each time' fit so many different things?
open_questions.why_open: Stairs, ages, tree rings and savings all follow it, at least roughly. Thinkers do not agree on why maths fits the world so well.

There are 10 grapes. If you eat two at a time, what numbers will be left on the plate each time?
Count the dots in this kolam, row by row. Do the rows follow a rule?
The lift is on floor 5 and going down. What will it show next? And then?
What is something at home that gets a little bigger every day? What gets a little smaller?

jokes.j: What did 9 say to 10 in the countdown?

maths.problem: Lamps stand on the steps of a house. The top step has 1 lamp, the next has 2, the next 3, the next 4. How many lamps does step 6 need?
maths.explain: The rule is one more each step. Step 5 needs 5. Step 6 needs one more than that, which is 6.
maths.context: In the Staircase Test you guessed a row of chana before building it. This uses the same idea with lamps on the steps of a house.
maths.why_maths: Knowing the rule tells you how many lamps to carry before you walk down, so you make one trip and not two.

maths.problem: A button is on 3 on the number track. It hops two more, four times. Which numbers does it land on? Where does it end?
maths.explain: Two more than 3 is 5. Then 7, then 9, then 11. Four hops, so four numbers after the start.
maths.context: In the Number Track activity you hopped a button two boxes at a time. This asks where the button ends after four hops from 3.
maths.why_maths: Equal hops along a track are the first way to add the same number again and again.

chart.title: Start on 3. Hop two more, four times.

maths.problem: A tin holds 12 murukkus. The family eats 2 each day. How many are left after 3 days? On which day is the tin empty?
maths.answer: 6 are left after 3 days. The tin is empty on day 6.
maths.explain: The rule is two fewer each day: 12, 10, 8, 6. That is 3 days. Carry on: 4, 2, 0. That is 3 more days, so day 6.
maths.context: In the Staircase Test you built rows that shrank by two each time. This uses the same rule on a tin of murukkus.
maths.why_maths: A shrinking pattern tells you when something will run out, before it happens.

maths.problem: The top half of a kolam has rows of 7, 5, 3 and 1 dots. How many dots is that altogether?
maths.explain: Add the rows. 7 and 5 is 12. 12 and 3 is 15. 15 and 1 is 16.
maths.context: In the 7 to 1 kolam you put down rows of dots that shrank by two each time. This asks how many dots four of those rows use.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the rows tells you how many dots to expect, so you can check that none was missed.

chart.title: Four rows of a 7 to 1 kolam

maths.problem: Someone copied the right-hand page numbers of a book: 1, 3, 5, 8, 9. One number is wrong. Which one, and what should it be?
maths.answer: The 8 is wrong. It should be 7.
maths.explain: The rule is two more each time. Two more than 5 is 7, not 8. And two more than 7 is 9, which fits the last number.
maths.context: In the Pattern Hunt you read only the right-hand page numbers of a book. This uses their rule to catch a copying mistake.
maths.why_maths: When you know the rule of a pattern, a number that breaks the rule stands out. That is how mistakes in lists are found.
