warmup.q: Clap once, then twice, then three times. Growing or repeating?
warmup.a: Growing. Each turn is one clap more.

warmup.q: A staircase has rows of 1, 2, 3, 4. How many in row 6?
warmup.a: 6. Row 5 has 5, and row 6 has one more.

roots.context: We built staircases of chana and hopped along a number track. Now let us think about what one small step can do.

deep_truth.truth: In the Staircase Test, each row had only one more chana than the row before. One chana is a very small change. But you kept to the same rule, and row 7 had seven. No row made a big jump. A big number can come from one small step, done again and again.
deep_truth.habit: When we see something big, we think something big must have made it. We forget the small steps underneath. And the tidy rule, the same step every time, is ours. We chose it and we kept to it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Staircase Test, the first row had 1 chana and the seventh had 7, and every row added only 1. With two more each time, the fifth row already had 10.

three.who_am_i: You were once small enough to sleep on one arm. You did not grow in one big jump. You grew a tiny bit each day, too little for anyone to see.
three.what_is_life: A teak tree adds one thin ring of wood each year. A coconut palm opens about one new leaf each month. Living beings build themselves one small step at a time.
three.what_is_this_world: The Moon shows a little more of its bright face each night, for about two weeks. Then it shows a little less each night. The sky has growing and shrinking patterns too.

roots.thread: Start with an empty floor. Put down one chana. Then one more, and one more. Every number you know is made this way, from one small step done again and again. Change the step to two, and the same start gives a different staircase.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha says: do not think little of a small good deed. A water pot is filled drop by drop. In the same way, a wise person fills up with good, little by little.
teachings.link: A drop is 'one more each time'. Your staircase reached 7 in the same way, one chana at a time.

teachings.teaching: The Tao Te Ching says: a tower nine storeys high begins as a heap of earth. A journey of a thousand li begins under your feet. A li is an old Chinese measure, about half a kilometre.
teachings.link: The tower and the journey are both made of small steps that are the same. That is a growing pattern.

teachings.source: Tamil proverb: Siru thuli peru vellam
teachings.teaching: An old Tamil saying goes: small drops make a great flood.
teachings.link: Anyone who has watched the monsoon fill a street has seen it. A flood is one drop more, a great many times.

science.text: A child of about six grows roughly 6 centimetres taller in a year. Spread over the days, that is less than a quarter of a millimetre a day. Nobody can see one day's growth. Everyone can see a year's.
Is the rule 'one more each time' out in the world, or did people make it to describe the world? Thinkers still argue about this.

other_view.who: Many scientists who study how things change
other_view.view: They say this is only half the story. Some big changes are sudden. A balloon pops. A glass falls and breaks. And real things almost never add exactly the same amount each time. A teak tree makes a wide ring in a wet year and a thin ring in a dry year. They say the neat rule is in our maths, and the tree only comes close to it.

practice.title: A breath that grows and shrinks
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. Breathe in while I count to 1, and breathe out. Now breathe in while I count 1, 2. Next breath, 1, 2, 3. Then 4. Now we come back down: 3, then 2, then 1. Open your eyes. Which breath felt the biggest? Did any breath make a big jump from the one before?
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Breathe in for a count of 1. Next breath, count to 2. Then 3, then 4. Now come back down: 3, 2, 1. Did any breath make a big jump?

ask: You are taller than last year. On which day did you grow?
Is 'one more each time' in the chana, or in the one who lays them down?
What is something big that was made by many small steps? What is something big that happened all at once?
Does a staircase of numbers ever have a last step?

how_we_found_out.context: How do we know that small children can think about patterns that grow? This card tells the true story of a study of 400 four-year-olds.
how_we_found_out.story: For many years, when researchers studied small children and patterns, they nearly always used repeating patterns, such as red, blue, red, blue. Patterns that grow, such as one block, two blocks, three blocks, were hardly studied at this age. So very little was known about what young children make of them. In 2019 Nore Wijns and four other researchers at the University of Leuven in Belgium set out to fill this gap. They worked with 400 four-year-olds, one child at a time. Each child was given both kinds of pattern, repeating and growing. The child was asked to carry a pattern on, to make the same pattern with other things, and to show how the pattern was built. The researchers also gave each child eight number tasks. They found that the kind of pattern and the kind of task both changed how well the children did. They also found that children who did well on most of the pattern tasks tended to do well with numbers. Growing patterns are now studied alongside repeating ones.
how_we_found_out.who: Nore Wijns, Joke Torbeyns, Merel Bakker, Bert De Smedt and Lieven Verschaffel
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: For small children, the only patterns worth studying are repeating patterns. The 2019 study showed this was too narrow. Four-year-olds could work on growing patterns too, and how they did on patterns went together with how they did with numbers.

Teak (Tectona grandis) forms distinct, datable annual rings, first reported by Brandis in 1879: Sinha, S. K. and others, 'Tree-ring analysis of teak from Western Ghats of India as a tool to determine drought years', Emirates Journal of Food and Agriculture. False rings in teak are linked to drought years (studies of teak in Thailand and India).

Coconut palm (Cocos nucifera) produces about 12 to 14 leaves a year: Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, Agritech portal, coconut botany. Rates vary with climate and soil, so leaf scars give only a rough age.

Kolam dot grids named by their dot counts, for example '7 - 1 parallel dots (neer pulli)': start with 7 dots, leave one dot at both ends, stop at 1 (Kamala's Corner kolam pages, kolangal.kamalascorner.com).

Gopuccha yati (phrases that taper like a cow's tail) and srotovaha yati (phrases that widen like a river) in Muthuswami Dikshitar's 'Tyagaraja Yoga Vaibhavam', raga Ananda Bhairavi: karnatik.com glossary for the terms; lyrical-thyagaraja.blogspot.com (2 November 2009) for this song.
Navaratri Golu: the number of steps is odd, commonly 3, 5, 7, 9 or 11 (National Library Board Singapore, BiblioAsia, 'Navaratri Golu: The Hindu Festival of Dolls', 2019).

Moon phases: the lit fraction grows from 0 at new moon to 100 percent at full moon, and not by equal amounts each night (US Naval Observatory, 'Phases of the Moon and Percent of the Moon Illuminated').
Child growth: about 6 to 7 centimetres a year from about age 6 (KidsHealth, 'Growth and Your 6- to 12-Year-Old').

Dhammapada 122, translated by Acharya Buddharakkhita: 'Drop by drop is the water pot filled.' Tao Te Ching 64, translated by Gia-Fu Feng and Jane English: a terrace nine stories high begins with a pile of earth; a journey of a thousand miles starts under one's feet.
Solkattu syllables ta (one), ta ka (two), ta ki ta (three), ta ka di mi (four): standard South Indian rhythm practice.
Aryabhata, Aryabhatiya (499 CE), Ganitapada: the rule for the partial sum of a series that goes up in equal steps (multiply the sum of the first and last terms by half the number of terms).

playtest: Walked through every flow as a parent and one child in a flat. The Staircase Test needs about 60 chana if each old staircase is swept up before the next: 28 for rows 1 to 7, 30 for rows 2 to 10 and 25 for 9 down to 1. Chana roll, so work on newspaper or a mat. What Is My Rule? was checked for every pair of cards: with starts from 8 to 12 the button stays on the track for four hops under every rule. All 16 Fill the Gap cards were checked by working each one out. In the stretch puzzle, 20 chana cannot make a full staircase (15, then 21), and two staircases of 4 rows fit into a block of 20. Step minutes add up to each part's minutes. Facts looked up on the web while writing: the 2019 study of 400 four-year-olds (abstract only), yearly rings in teak and Brandis 1879, the 12 to 14 leaves a year of a coconut palm, the '7 to 1' way of naming kolam dots, the odd number of Golu steps, the Moon's lit part, how fast a six-year-old grows, Dhammapada 122, Tao Te Ching 64, the Tamil proverb and Aryabhata's rule for adding a series. The shrinking and growing lines in Dikshitar's song rest on one music blog plus a glossary of the terms, so a musician should confirm it. Not looked up: that right-hand pages of books carry odd numbers, that bus tickets are numbered in order, the countdown at Sriharikota, the ten bowling pins, and the Karthigai Deepam details in the story. That the researchers in the 2019 study worked at the University of Leuven comes from the paper's archive address, not from the paper itself.
